citation: Law YW, Lok RHT, Chiang B, Lai CCS, Tsui SHM, Chung PYJ, Leung SC. Effects of Community-Based Caring Contact in Reducing Thwarted Belongingness Among Postdischarge Young Adults With Self-Harm: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Formative Research. 2023;7:e43526. doi:10.2196/43526.
title: Effects of Community-Based Caring Contact in Reducing Thwarted Belongingness Among Postdischarge Young Adults With Self-Harm: Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: Pragmatic randomized controlled trial evaluating a self-help mobile app, with or without volunteer support, as an adjunct to treatment as usual for postdischarge adults aged 18–45 with self-harm or suicide attempts.
population: postdischarge adults aged 18-45 with self-harm or suicide attempts in Hong Kong
setting: four Hong Kong hospital emergency departments
intervention_or_exposure: mobile app plus volunteer support plus treatment as usual
mobile app plus treatment as usual
uncertainty: The article describes the findings as preliminary/formative and recommends cautious implementation.
Attrition and disruptions to recruitment/follow-up limit precision and generalizability.

evidence_claims.statement: In this small pragmatic RCT (n=40), adding volunteer care to a self-help mobile app and treatment as usual was associated with improved service compliance during postdischarge follow-up.
evidence_claims.population: postdischarge adults aged 18-45 with self-harm or suicide attempts in Hong Kong
evidence_claims.intervention_or_exposure: mobile app plus volunteer support plus treatment as usual

provenance.source_span: The abstract reports 40 participants and improved service compliance when volunteer care was blended with the app.

evidence_claims.statement: The authors report that reductions in perceived burdensomeness and thwarted belongingness in the caring-contact condition were linked to transient improvements in hopelessness and suicide-related outcomes, but the small formative sample limits certainty.
evidence_claims.population: postdischarge adults aged 18-45 with self-harm or suicide attempts in Hong Kong
evidence_claims.intervention_or_exposure: mobile app plus volunteer support plus treatment as usual

provenance.locator: JMIR article, Abstract Results and Discussion
provenance.source_span: The paper links changes in interpersonal constructs to transient improvements and explicitly frames implementation cautiously.

evidence_claims.statement: The authors conclude that the app-plus-volunteer strategy may cautiously strengthen continuity of care after hospital discharge, while emphasizing the formative nature of the evidence.
evidence_claims.population: postdischarge adults aged 18-45 with self-harm or suicide attempts in Hong Kong
evidence_claims.intervention_or_exposure: mobile app plus volunteer support plus treatment as usual
evidence_claims.method: author interpretation of pragmatic randomized controlled trial

provenance.source_span: The conclusion recommends only cautious implementation of the combined strategy.

limitations: Recruitment/follow-up disruptions and attrition reduce confidence in estimates.
The study does not justify individual suicide-risk scoring.
applicability: Potentially relevant to continuity-of-care programmes for postdischarge adults with self-harm in similar health-system settings.
Requires larger confirmatory studies before strong effectiveness claims.
safety_boundaries: Do not use study group averages to calculate a person’s suicide-risk percentage.
Do not infer that the app/volunteer intervention replaces professional clinical care.
